Keywords: warehouse size, auto-suspend, credit consumption, idle warehouse
Guidance: An oversized warehouse left without auto-suspend burns credits every minute it's idle; warehouse size should match workload, not be set once and forgotten.
Do: Set AUTO_SUSPEND to a short interval (60-300s) and start with the smallest warehouse size that meets query SLAs, scaling up only when justified.
Don't: Leave a Large or X-Large warehouse running 24/7 with auto-suspend disabled.
Example: ALTER WAREHOUSE compute_wh SET AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

Keywords: clustering key, micro-partition, pruning, query performance
Guidance: On very large tables, poor natural ordering means Snowflake can't prune micro-partitions effectively, scanning far more data than a query actually needs.
Do: Define a clustering key on large tables whose queries commonly filter on a specific low-cardinality-ish column (e.g. date), and monitor clustering depth.
Don't: Add a clustering key to every table regardless of size or query pattern -- reclustering itself costs credits.

Keywords: snowpipe, continuous ingestion, micro-batch, cloud storage event
Guidance: Batch-loading files on a fixed schedule (e.g. hourly COPY INTO) adds unnecessary latency for near-real-time use cases when Snowpipe can auto-ingest as files land in cloud storage.
Do: Use Snowpipe with cloud storage event notifications for continuous, low-latency ingestion instead of scheduled batch loads.
Don't: Run a scheduled COPY INTO every hour when the use case actually needs near-real-time data availability.
Example: CREATE PIPE my_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS COPY INTO my_table FROM @my_stage;

Topic: Query profile review for expensive queries
Keywords: query profile, query history, credit usage, expensive query
Guidance: Without reviewing the Query Profile / ACCOUNT_USAGE views regularly, a handful of runaway or badly-written queries can dominate warehouse credit consumption unnoticed.
Do: Regularly review QUERY_HISTORY / query profiles for the most expensive queries by credits and optimize or schedule them off-peak.
Don't: Never review query cost/credit consumption until the monthly bill is already a surprise.
Example: SELECT query_text, credits_used_cloud_services FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history ORDER BY credits_used_cloud_services DESC LIMIT 20;

Keywords: time travel, data_retention_time_in_days, undrop, historical data
Guidance: The default Time Travel retention (1 day on Standard edition) may not cover the window needed to recover from a delayed-discovery data quality incident.
Do: Set DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS deliberately per table/database based on how long you need to be able to UNDROP or query historical state.
Don't: Assume Time Travel covers an incident discovered a week after the bad change with only the 1-day default retention.

Keywords: rbac, role hierarchy, grants, least privilege
Guidance: Granting SYSADMIN or ACCOUNTADMIN broadly for convenience means far more users than necessary can modify warehouses, databases, and account-level settings.
Do: Design a custom role hierarchy scoped to least privilege, reserving ACCOUNTADMIN for a small, audited set of users.
Don't: Grant ACCOUNTADMIN to application service accounts or most engineers for convenience.
Example: GRANT ROLE analyst_role TO USER jdoe;

Keywords: zero-copy clone, dev environment, clone database
Guidance: Physically copying a multi-terabyte production database to create a dev/test environment wastes storage and time when Snowflake's zero-copy clone creates an instant, storage-efficient copy-on-write clone.
Do: Use CREATE ... CLONE to spin up dev/test/QA environments from production data instantly without duplicating storage.
Don't: Run a full ETL/export-import cycle to replicate production data into a dev environment.

Keywords: result cache, query result reuse, 24 hour cache
Guidance: Not understanding that Snowflake automatically reuses cached results for identical repeated queries (within 24h, unchanged data) can lead to unnecessary warehouse compute for benchmarking or repeated dashboard queries.
Do: Be aware of and design around result caching when benchmarking query performance, and note it can make a warehouse resize look like a bigger win than it is.
Don't: Benchmark 'query performance improvements' without accounting for result cache hits skewing the numbers.

Guidance: A single-cluster warehouse queues additional concurrent queries once it's saturated, causing dashboard/BI tool latency spikes during peak concurrent usage.
Do: Enable multi-cluster warehouses (auto-scale mode) for workloads with unpredictable concurrent query bursts, like BI dashboards.
Don't: Run a single fixed-size warehouse for a BI workload with highly variable concurrent user counts.
Example: ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1 MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4 SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD';

Topic: File sizing for COPY INTO performance
Keywords: copy into, file size, parallel load, staged files
Guidance: Loading many very small files (or a few very large ones) into Snowflake underuses the parallel loading architecture, which is optimized for files in the 100-250MB compressed range.
Do: Stage files sized roughly 100-250MB compressed before COPY INTO to maximize load parallelism.
Don't: Load thousands of small (KB-sized) files or a handful of multi-GB files without considering Snowflake's optimal file size range.

Keywords: resource monitor, credit quota, spend cap
Guidance: Without a resource monitor, a runaway query or misconfigured pipeline can consume unlimited credits with no automatic circuit breaker.
Do: Set resource monitors with notification and suspend actions at defined credit thresholds per warehouse or account.
Don't: Run production warehouses with no resource monitor or spend cap configured.
Example: CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR rm1 WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 1000 TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;

Keywords: network policy, ip allowlist, account security
Guidance: Leaving an account reachable from any IP address widens the attack surface for credential-stuffing attempts against Snowflake's public endpoint.
Do: Configure a network policy allowlisting known corporate/VPN IP ranges for account access.
Don't: Leave a Snowflake account with no network policy restricting source IP ranges.
